sections.h2: Closing charges Georgia sets on a seller
sections.html:
Only one seller charge is fixed by the state: the real estate transfer tax. Attorney fees, the loan payoff and any commission depend on your contract and lender, and vary with every deal.

Four items follow published rules you can look up ahead of time: transfer tax, the PT-61 filed with the deed, that year's property tax, and withholding on sellers who live outside Georgia. A table below puts them side by side.

A few days before closing, request the draft settlement statement and compare every line with your contract. Some costs can be shifted by agreement, which is why the wording counts.

sections.h2: How the Georgia transfer tax is figured
sections.html:
The tax scales with the price. You pay $1 for the first $1,000 or any piece of it, then 10 cents for every added $100 or fraction. See O.C.G.A. 48-6-1 through 48-6-10.

The law puts the tax on the person signing the deed or the person who gains from it, and in practice the seller is the one liable. Many contracts push it onto the buyer. A contract that says nothing leaves it on you, so check this clause first.

Think of it as a fee for moving title. It has no link to the annual property tax, and paying it does nothing for your county bill.

Each deed that qualifies travels with a PT-61, a declaration of the transfer for tax purposes. Whoever files fills it out in the clerks' authority PT-61 eFiling portal, prints it, and brings it to the Clerk of Superior Court along with the deed.

The deed cannot be recorded until the transfer tax is paid. After payment, a certification goes on the paperwork. Your closing firm usually prepares the form from the settlement figures, so you mainly need to confirm the sale and parcel details are right.

Customer support for the online filing system is at (800) 304-5174, or (404) 327-9760 for local callers. Taxability or exemption questions belong with the superior court clerk where the house sits.

What the clerk collects is shared by the state, the county and any city. Each year the clerk files a form called FA-RETT, due March 1, showing how the money was divided. That is paperwork on the clerk's side and does not alter your bill.

What matters to you is the certification on your deed showing the tax was paid. Before anyone leaves the table, have your settlement agent confirm both the PT-61 filing and the payment.

sections.h2: Property tax at a Georgia closing
sections.html:
Owning the house on January 1 makes you responsible for that full year's bill, even if you sell the next day. Partial-year owners get no refund from the state.

Any split between you and the buyer therefore comes from the contract. December 20 is the usual due date, but counties choose their own, and taxpayers get 60 days from billing. Fulton County, for instance, runs an earlier schedule, with the City of Atlanta's share due even sooner. Check yours.

Before closing:

  • Get the current balance from the county tax commissioner.
  • Confirm with the settlement agent how the contract divides the year.
  • Look for any county tax lien on the clerk's general execution docket, where such liens are recorded.

sections.h2: Does the intangible recording tax land on the seller?
sections.html:
This tax belongs to the buyer's new loan, a long-term note secured by real estate. It is $1.50 per $500 of the note or part of $500, and one note never pays more than $25,000.

The lender gets 90 days to record the security instrument and may bill the tax to the borrower. Clerks of Superior Court collect it in most places. In a list of 24 smaller counties, the tax commissioner or tax collector does the collecting instead. Paying off your own loan from the sale proceeds does not trigger it.

When the seller lives out of state, O.C.G.A. 48-7-128 requires the buyer to hold back 3% of the price, or 3% of the gain if the seller swears to it in an affidavit. The money is due by the end of the month following closing.

Exemptions include a principal residence under federal rules, prices below $20,000, and a transfer to a mortgagee in foreclosure with no added payment. Form IT-AFF3, the exemption certificate, is optional but helps the file. The state treats the charge as income tax withholding.

Georgia seller closing items at a glance
Closing itemRuleWho handles it
Transfer tax$1 per first $1,000, plus 10 cents per additional $100Seller by default; contract may shift it
PT-61 declarationOne form per applicable deed, filed onlineClosing office with the Clerk of Superior Court
Property taxOwner on January 1 owes the year; no partial-year refundContract proration and county tax commissioner
Intangible recording tax$1.50 per $500 of the note, $25,000 capLender, passed to borrower
Nonresident withholding3% of price or of sworn gainBuyer withholds and remits

Save the final settlement statement, the recorded deed details and any withholding statement from the buyer. A nonresident seller attaches the buyer's withholding return, or the equivalent document, to the Georgia income tax return to claim credit.

A Form 1099-S makes the sale reportable even when the gain is excludable, so use the settlement statement to check its figures.

  • Final settlement statement showing price, payoff and every charge.
  • The PT-61 copy and the clerk's certificate that transfer tax was paid, when provided.
  • Tax bill and proof of payment for the sale year.
  • Any Form G-2RP or similar statement of Georgia tax withheld.

The order is simple. You sign the deed and go through the settlement statement with the closing office. Your mortgage is paid from the proceeds, and the transfer tax is paid so the clerk can certify it before recording. The rest is your net, wired or handed to you.

Bring a government photo ID and the payoff details for any loan. If the house has more than one owner, every owner on title signs, so line up the co-owners ahead of time. Ask the closing office when you can expect your proceeds and whether any withholding will reduce them.

With a cash buyer there is no lender, no loan documents and no intangible tax, so the day goes faster. Transfer tax, PT-61 and the property tax split all still apply.

faqs.q: Who bears the transfer tax on a Georgia sale?
faqs.a: Seller, unless the contract shifts it to the buyer, which many do. A contract that says nothing leaves the cost with you.

faqs.q: What is the Georgia transfer tax rate?
faqs.a: $1 on the first $1,000 and 10 cents for each added $100, counting fractions in full. The rule sits in O.C.G.A. 48-6-1 through 48-6-10. Your settlement statement shows the dollar amount.

faqs.q: Can a seller get back property tax after leaving mid-year?
faqs.a: No. Whoever owns the home on January 1 carries the year, with no partial refund. Splitting it with the buyer is a matter for the contract.

faqs.q: Who files the PT-61 in Georgia?
faqs.a: Whoever files completes it through the clerks' authority online portal, one form per applicable deed. Check with your settlement agent that someone is preparing it and that it reaches the clerk with the deed.

faqs.q: Where do I ask about a transfer tax exemption?
faqs.a: Call the superior court clerk in the county where the property sits. That office handles taxability and exemption questions and certifies payment before recording.
